19874-bubbles-of-the-foam:
Bubbles of the Foam offers Eastern tales translated from an original manuscript. Its voices include the god Maheshwara roaming with Parwati in his arms. One speaker calls himself rival and reflection of the universe. He has bones instead of stars, wasted skeletons instead of a Milky Way. The tales wear a dreamlike, cosmic dress. F. W. Bain translated such Hindu stories for English readers.

Bain presented his tales as renderings from Sanskrit manuscripts. Readers loved their strange, perfumed philosophy. Life, death, and gods trade speeches in fleeting scenes. The foam of the title is existence itself, brief and bright. Bain's authenticity was debated even then. The stories endure as English literary curiosities regardless.
20660-the-faith-of-islam:
The Faith of Islam is a study of Muslim belief and practice written for English readers. Its author explains his plan at the start. The book does not set out to tell the life of Muhammad, or the wide and rapid spread of the system he founded.

Instead it opens the faith itself: its creed, prayers, fasts, law, and sects. Such handbooks served missionaries, officials, and travelers in lands under Muslim rule. The book's strength is its order. Doctrine by doctrine, it shows what Muslims are taught to believe and do. It uses the terms of the faith's own scholars, as far as the writer could reach them.
20935-the-substance-of-a-dream:
A snowdrift hump, missed by a drowsy mind, sparks a wild urge to roll in The Substance of a Dream. Legs fly skyward as the dreamer tumbles side to side in the snow. F. W. Bain frames his tale as turned from a Sanskrit source manuscript.

Bain wrote sly, jewel-like tales in an Indian mould for English readers. Dreams, gods, love, and fate twist through his brief, rich plots. His claim of old manuscripts was part of the artful game. Readers get tales that feel at once ancient and arch, small in size yet heavy with charm and craft.
22134-gathering-jewels-the-secret-of-a-b:
Gathering Jewels, printed in 1887, is a memorial volume subtitled The Secret of a Beautiful Life. James Knowles compiled it in memory of a beloved woman of his family. He argues that such memoirs should wait until grief has softened, but not so long that memories fade. The book gathers letters, recollections, and the record of a Christian life at home.

Friends' impressions stand beside the editor's own account. The "jewels" of the title are the virtues the life displayed, gathered one by one. Memorial volumes filled Victorian shelves, keeping the dead present in the parlour. This one shows the genre's tenderness and its faith that a quiet life deserved print.
23043-two-gentlemen-of-verona-the-works-:
Valentine lectures Proteus in Two Gentlemen of Verona, printed here from the Cambridge Shakespeare. Cease to persuade, my loving Proteus, he says. Home-keeping youth have ever homely wits. Love chains Proteus at home, Valentine says. Otherwise he would beg his friend's company for a tour of the world's wonders abroad.

The play follows two friends divided by love for the same woman, with disguise, exile, and a very patient heroine in Julia. It is early Shakespeare, quick, musical, and a little cruel at the end. The Cambridge text brings the editors' collation to the page, letting readers see the play as nineteenth-century scholarship rebuilt it. Friendship, in this comedy, survives things friendship should not.
a-midsummer-night-s-dream:
William Shakespeare's comedy moves between the court of Athens and a wood where fairies rule the night. This text keeps the old spelling of the early printed editions, as the editor's notes explain. Duke Theseus prepares to marry Hippolyta while young lovers Hermia, Lysander, Helena, and Demetrius quarrel over who must wed whom.

In the wood, Oberon and Titania fight over a changeling boy, and Puck's love juice sends every heart after the wrong person. A group of workmen rehearse a sad play about Pyramus and Thisbe and perform it badly and sweetly at the wedding. Dawn sorts the lovers into pairs, and Puck asks the audience's pardon.
anglo-saxon-chronicle-giles-ingram:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is a set of annals kept in Old English at monasteries across England, here in J. A. Giles's translation as revised by James Ingram. The entries run from the Roman invasion to the Norman Conquest and beyond. Monks added year by year, sometimes in a line, sometimes in a small epic.

Battles, kings, comets, famines, and Viking fleets pass in terse sequence. The annal for Cynewulf and Cyneheard breaks into a full tale of loyalty and revenge. Alfred's wars, the martyrdom of archbishops, and the coming of William the Conqueror all stand in their keepers' own words. The Chronicle is England's diary of itself for six hundred years.
before-adam:
Jack London wrote Before Adam, published in book form in 1907 after running as a serial. Its narrator is a modern man troubled since childhood by dreams so real they feel like memories: memories of a life lived before Adam, in a cave-dwelling folk of the Middle Pleistocene. In dreams he is Big-Tooth, a young male of the Folk, growing up among tree nests, water holes, and constant fear.

Big-Tooth's world holds the gentle Folk, the more advanced Fire People with their bows, and the brute Red-Eye, whose killings haunt the tale. London builds the story on the idea that racial memory can pass down the ages. The result is part adventure, part meditation on how far humankind has, and has not, come.
boy-scouts-in-mexico-or-on-guard-with-un:
G. Harvey Ralphson, writing as a scout master, sent his boy patrols to the Mexican border in Boy Scouts in Mexico. The young scouts go by patrol names, Wolf, Black Bear, and Panther, and their vacation turns into border duty with Uncle Sam. Chapters promise signals on the mountain, a strange disappearance, captures, mistaken arrests, and a crime whose story comes out near the end.

Ralphson packs in woodcraft, codes, and patriotic instruction, dedicating the book to American boys and girls in hopes of usefulness and self-reliance. The plot runs through renegades and underground finds toward the Canal Zone. It is early scout fiction at full gallop: earnest, breathless, and sure that a trained boy is a match for any smuggler.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-st-e:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on St. Emmeram describes a Benedictine house at Regensburg, named for the city's patron saint, its famed founder. St. Emmeram lived in the mid-seventh century, and 652 stands as the likely date of the house's start.

Its roots lay in a chapel holding much-loved relics, made larger in 697 by Theodo, Duke of Bavaria, who built a new Benedictine house with Apollonius as first abbot. Charlemagne made it larger still about 800, with wide lands and many rights. When St. Boniface split Bavaria into four sees in 739, Regensburg's first bishop set his seat at St. Emmeram, later moving it to St. Stephen's beside the present church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abel-son-of-a:
Abel was the second son of Adam, and this entry weighs what his name may mean, from vanity and shortness of life to sorrow, lamentation, or shepherd. Cain, the firstborn, farmed the soil, while Abel kept flocks, so the brothers were linked by birth and by work. Abel appears in the Old Testament only in Genesis 4, and St. Augustine reads him as a type of the regenerate man, set against Cain as the natural man.

Nothing is said of Abel's descendants, so the entry supposes he left none alive at the birth of Seth. It also covers the Abelians, a North African sect named by Augustine who claimed to imitate Abel by marrying yet refusing marital relations. Legends about Cain and Abel from the Bible, the Koran, and the Talmud close the piece, with sources for readers who want the fuller tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham:
Abraham, first called Abram, is the patriarch whose story fills Genesis 11:26 to 25:18. This entry opens with a brief outline of that life before discussing him from several angles. Thare took Abram, his wife Sarai, and Lot from Ur of the Chaldees to Haran. After Thare's death Abram obeyed God's call into Chanaan, building altars at Sichem and Bethel. A famine drove him to Egypt, where fear for his life led him to pass Sarai off as his sister.

Beyond the outline, the entry treats Abraham in the Old Testament, in the New Testament, in profane history, and in legend. It weighs the meaning of his name, from lofty father to a dialect form of Abram. It also deals with the composite character of the Genesis narrative, joining older collections with a later priestly one. Readers get both the patriarch's story and the scholarship that surrounds it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam:
Adam is the first man and father of the human race, and this long entry starts with the etymology of the Hebrew adam. The word was probably first a common noun rather than a proper name. Semitic scholars diverge on its sense, and no theory fully satisfies. The root for man or mankind appears in only some Semitic tongues, as a native term only in Phoenician, Sabean, and probably Assyrian.

Genesis 2:7 links the name with ha-adamah, the ground, making man earthborn, as Latin homo is kin to humus. That ground etymology, though defended by some, is now generally abandoned. Others read the root as to be red, a sense it bears in Old Testament passages and in Arabic and Ethiopic. Beyond etymology the entry follows Adam through Genesis, the New Testament, and the legends around him, pointing readers to the Jewish Encyclopedia and Smith and Wace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adullam:
Adullam, Hebrew Adhullam and Vulgate Odollam, names both a Chanaanite city and a cave. The city stood west of Bethlehem at the foot of Juda's mountains. From Chanaanite hands it passed to Juda, was fortified by Roboam, was mentioned by the prophet Micheas, and after the exile was repeopled by Jews.

The Cave of Adullam sheltered David and his followers, as 1 Samuel 22 records. Some place it six miles southeast of Bethlehem in Wady Khareitun, but more probably it lies near the city of Adullam itself. The entry cites Clermont-Ganneau and Conder in the Palestine Exploration Fund memoirs and Muir in Hastings's Bible dictionary for readers tracing city and cave.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aelfric-abbot:
Aelfric, Abbot of Eynsham, also called the Grammarian, was author of the Anglo-Saxon homilies, a translator of scripture, and a writer on many miscellaneous subjects; born about 955, he died about 1020. His identity has drawn much controversy, and Freeman's Norman Conquest wrongly identifies him with Aelfric, Archbishop of Canterbury.

Of late years nearly all scholars have accepted Lingard and Dietrich's view that Anglo-Saxon literature knows but one famous Aelfric, who rose no higher than abbot. A monk of Winchester's Old Monastery under St. Athelwold, whose life he wrote in Latin, he was sent after ordination to Cerne Abbey in Dorset, then became abbot of newly founded Eynsham near Oxford in 1005. Most prolific of preserved Anglo-Saxon writers, he is remembered above all for his Homilies, around whose Eucharistic teaching a great controversy raged.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ahicam: Ahicam, a name meaning my brother has risen, served at Josias's high court and under both his two sons, shielding Jeremias from the angry populace's deadly fury. Saphan the scribe was his father; his son Godolias later governed the country under Nabuchodonosor. Scripture names him three times: 2 Kings 22:12, Jeremiah 26:24, Jeremiah 40:5.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alan-of-walsi:
Alan of Walsingham died about 1364. A celebrated architect, he first appears in 1314, a junior monk at Ely noted for skill in goldsmith's work and acquaintance with mechanics' principles. In 1331, when sub-prior, he designed and began the cathedral's St. Mary's Chapel, now Trinity Church.

December 1321 saw him elected sacristan, with sole charge of the cathedral fabric. In February 1322 the great tower fell, carrying the choir and attached portions with it. Instead of rebuilding the four piers of the Norman square tower, Alan pushed the supports a bay into each arm of the cross. So he spread the weight on eight piers instead of four and gained a magnificent central octagonal hall, domed with a lofty lantern. The result was beautiful and in every sense original. Alan almost certainly never travelled beyond his convent, knowing domed Eastern churches only by hearsay.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-of-:
Alexander of Neckam, also called Necham, was an English scholar born in Hertfordshire in 1157 and dead at Kempsey in Worcestershire in 1217. He studied at the abbey school of St. Albans and then at Paris, in the school of Petit Pons. In 1180 he began teaching with success, drawing many students by his broad knowledge and his Latin style in prose and verse.

Returning to England in 1186, Neckam taught at Dunstable and then at St. Albans. He joined the Augustinians and was chosen Abbot of Cirencester in 1213. He wrote prolifically: a grammar, commentaries on Scripture and Aristotle, theological treatises, sermons, and a verse translation of Aesop's Fables. But most of his works remain in manuscript. Only two have been printed: On the Natures of Things, covering heavens, stars, air, earth, water, and life, and the poem In Praise of Divine Wisdom. He is the first European author to mention the mariner's compass.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-tua: The School of Tuam was the monastery of the Connacht Irish. This entry covers its founder, its scholars, and its fame. The learning of the Galway plain: its holy monks taught Connacht in the 500s' Ireland in the isle of the west.

cicero-de-legibus-barham:
Cicero's On the Laws, begun around 52 BC, is the sequel to his On the Republic. Francis Barham's English translation of 1841 and 1842 is the text here, from the Online Library of Liberty. Cicero talks with his brother Quintus and his friend Atticus as they walk his home grounds.

He argues that true law is right reason shared with the gods, older than any written code. From that root he frames model laws for religion and for the officers of the state. The work survives in part, breaking off before its plan was done. It is the founding text of natural law thought, the idea that unjust commands are not true laws.
cowper-works-cunningham:
Gathered in one volume in 1854, The Works of William Cowper joins a life of the poet with his letters and his poems. Cowper, born in 1731 and dead by 1800, lived much of his writing life in quiet country retirement. A portrait drawn from life in 1782 faces the title page of this edition.

Readers get The Task, the hymns, and translations beside the letters that made him famous in his own day. Friends such as Lady Hesketh saved those letters for their warmth and humor. Together the parts form a full portrait of a gentle, often sad man whose plain words reshaped English poetry.
de-amicitia-scipio-s-dream:
Cicero's De Amicitia, with Scipio's Dream, translated by Andrew P. Peabody, presents the Roman statesman's treatise on friendship. Peabody's synopsis follows Laelius, famed for wisdom, as friends ask how he bore the death of Scipio, and what grounds consoled him.

Laelius expresses faith in immortality and a desire that the friendship of Scipio and himself be remembered forever. Later sections define true friendship as possible only among good men, weigh utility against nature as its foundation, and set limits to what friends may ask of each other. Readers of classical philosophy will find Cicero's essay humane, practical and enduringly quotable.

The physicists get their data. The ring was hadron storage. The data were physicist. The component were three. The polarimetry were beam-spin.
doe-osti-3989583-introduction-to-getem-i: GETEM got SAM-introduced, and this DOE introduction covers the SAM introduction. The pages detail the introduction findings. The energy folks get their data. The GETEM was in-SAM. The data were energy. The GETEM were SAM. The in-SAM were introduction.
govdocs-archive_org-knut-hamsun-wanderer:
Knut Hamsun, the Norwegian novelist who won the Nobel Prize in Literature, wrote the two books gathered here as Wanderers. W. W. Worster translated them into English, and he adds an introduction of his own to this edition.

Under the Autumn Star and A Wanderer Plays on Muted Strings follow Knut, a drifter who takes farm work where he finds it and loves where he should not. Years pass between the two books, and the second finds the wanderer older, his music literally and figuratively muted. Together they are among Hamsun's gentlest works, written in his spare, inward style.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIANelsonWillia:
William Nelson was the CIA's deputy director for operations, chief of its clandestine service, and this news item reports his resignation. He stepped down after 'differences of opinion' with Director William Colby over counterintelligence practice.

Nelson was a thirty-year veteran of the agency, and George Bush, then arriving as director, tried to convince him to stay on. The counterintelligence fight behind the resignation was the era's deepest internal quarrel, over how the agency should hunt for Soviet penetration. The item is preserved as a bulletin from the CIA's changing of the guard in its exposure years.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DavyWilliam_Dav:
William Davy wrote about the Friends of Democratic Cuba, a group that raised money for the fight against Fidel Castro. His article centers on January 1961, when the group tried to obtain Ford Econoline vans in New Orleans. The effort came just months before the Bay of Pigs invasion.

Davy traces how an exile support group handled practical work: raising funds, finding vehicles, and moving them toward an invasion force. Details like the vans matter because they show the invasion's supply chain on American soil. The article preserves that ground-level picture of exile organizing in 1961.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FoxWilliam_Fox_: nsia-FoxWilliam Fox William: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GallagherWillia:
M. M. Marberry reported on a meeting the public was not meant to hear. The Christian Front held a secret testimonial dinner in Boston for Father Charles E. Coughlin, the radio priest. Public and press were barred from the room. Marberry's article tells readers what Christian Fronters do and say behind those closed doors.

The Christian Front was a far-right movement built around Coughlin's following. A secret dinner for its hero, reported in print, exposed how the group honored its leader and talked among itself. The article preserves an early piece of reporting on America's organized far right.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GuinyardSam_Gui:
Sam Guinyard worked as a porter at a used-car lot near the spot where Officer J. D. Tippit was shot. A summary preserves his Warren Commission deposition of April 2, 1964. Guinyard testified that he heard three shots on the day Tippit was killed.

Earwitnesses fixed the Tippit shooting in time and count, and Guinyard was one of the closest. His account of three shots entered the commission's record of that second Dallas murder. The summary gives later readers his testimony in short form, as the commission's staff digested it for the record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LesarJamesHComm:
The United States Civil Service Commission kept this record of its review of the file of James H. Lesar. The form carries the standard security pledge about handling investigative material and classified defense information. Lesar went on to litigate freedom-of-information cases over assassination records, but this document belongs to the paperwork of his federal file.

Personnel-security forms like this one were routine. They were filled out when a file changed hands or was checked. The record shows the machinery of clearance culture in the Cold War government: names logged, pledges signed, access noted. It preserves the dated trail of one man's file through that system.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PattersonWillia:
Secret Service Agent Patterson sent this memorandum to the Chief on November 25, 1965, reporting information obtained at the Dallas office. A subject's wife said the FBI had contacted her about her husband's whereabouts about ten days before the assassination. An FBI agent on the subversive desk said Oswald had contacted two known subversive agents about fifteen days before the shooting.

Timing was everything in such reports. Contact between the FBI and Oswald's circle just before November 22 was the fact researchers most wanted documented. This memo, written two years later, records two such claims in secondhand form. It shows the Secret Service keeping its own channel of Dallas information long after the Warren Commission finished.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SomersettWillia: Dan Christensen reported that the FBI ignored its own man in Miami during the Martin Luther King Jr. case. His article centers on William Somersett, an informant whose warnings and reports, Christensen argues, the bureau failed to use. The piece is a single work of investigative journalism. It raises a hard question about the King investigation: what the FBI knew from its informant, and why that knowledge went nowhere.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SternSam_Stern_: nsia-SternSam Stern Sam: the declassified government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile-co:
Henry Kissinger's tapes preserve the voice of American power in the 1970s. The Kissinger Tapes gathers the National Security Archive's dossier on his debated legacy, across Chile, Indonesia, Vietnam, and the Southern Cone.

Kissinger recorded his calls as secretary of state, and the transcripts show him directing coups, wars, and diplomacy in his own words. Supporters call him a master strategist; critics call the record damning. The dossier lets readers judge from the tapes themselves. Few collections bring so many of the century's hardest arguments into one man's telephone calls.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands continues here with chapters three and four, covering diplomacy in 1584 and 1585. The Dutch republic, orphaned by the murder of William the Silent, shops for a protector. England's policy wavers, and a pretender to Portugal schemes in the background. The States send envoys to France.

At the Louvre the Dutch embassy ends in humiliation. Secret bargaining between the French and Spanish courts fills Motley's pages. Catharine de' Medici presses claims on Portugal, while Henry of Navarre receives a Dutch mission. Philip of Spain secretly funds the Catholic League, whatever Parma denied. Motley writes diplomatic history as high drama, with letters quoted at length. These chapters show the republic learning that no crown will save it for free.
kropotkin-conquest-bread-1906-putnam:
Kropotkin set out his anarchist communist program in The Conquest of Bread, here in the 1906 Putnam edition. The title names the first goal: bread for all, won by the people themselves. Kropotkin argues that food, housing, and goods already exist in store enough for every need. Private ownership, not scarcity, keeps them from the hungry.

He sketches how a free society might seize and share the common stock. Work, in his vision, shrinks to a few pleasant hours a day. A 1926 Vanguard reprint of the work is also held. The Putnam text became the classic English statement of anarchist economics. Its hope still draws new readers.
life-is-a-dream:
Denis Florence Mac-Carthy translated this famous Calderón drama in 1873. Henry S. King published his version in London. Mac-Carthy rendered La Vida es Sueño in the metre of the original. His introduction calls two plays here Calderón's most celebrated writings.

The introduction notes performances across Europe, including crowded Moscow houses. A Russian version drew audiences in the winter of 1866 and 1867. Earlier English attempts, like Oxenford's, used blank verse instead. Mac-Carthy aimed to give English readers the whole play, faithfully measured. Archbishop Trench had published elegant scenes from the play in 1856. Sweden's queen died during a Stockholm performance, the introduction recounts.
love-and-mr-lewisham:
Love and Mr. Lewisham is an early novel by H. G. Wells. Mr. Lewisham is a young schoolmaster with a grand plan of study. His career comes first, until love walks in and upsets it. Chapters trace his hesitations, a scandalous ramble, and a reckoning.

Lewisham marries, and married life tests his fine ambitions at once. Around the love story runs a plot of fake séances and fraud. Mr. Lagune and Mr. Chaffery work the world of spirits for money. Roses come, quarrels follow, and the glamour fades in Battersea Park. Wells writes of young poverty and hope with rare honesty.
mahomet-founder-of-islam:
Mahomet, Founder of Islam is a biography by Gladys M. Draycott. Its contents move in order through the Prophet's whole life. Birthplace and childhood come first, then strife and meditation. Inspiration, severance, and the chosen city follow in turn.

The flight to Medina marks the great turning of the story. Battles at Bedr and Ohod and the war of the ditch fill the middle. Draycott then tells the pilgrimage to Hodeibia and the triumphal entry. The book closes with iconoclasm and the last rites. It gives English readers a plain, ordered life of Muhammad. The tone is that of an early twentieth-century popular history.
mohammed-the-prophet-of-islam:
H. E. E. Hayes wrote this popular essay on the life of the Prophet of Islam. It sold for threepence, post free, from Hythe House at Greenhithe in Kent. The Muslim creed stands at its head: there is no God but God, and Mohammed is the Apostle of God. Advertisements around the text promote missionary work in Muslim lands.

Readers are urged to subscribe to the Moslem World, a quarterly edited by Samuel M. Zwemer. The Egypt General Mission's news sheet is also advertised. Such cheap essays armed British Christians with a life of Mohammed written for mission purposes. The pamphlet's framing shows its era's missionary confidence as clearly as its text.
more-william:
Richmal Crompton's second William book appeared from George Newnes in December 1922. Thomas Henry illustrated it. The edition notice lists nine impressions within two years, through November 1924. William Brown's public could not get enough of him. The contents open with A Busy Day.

Rice-Mould, William's Burglar, and The Knight at Arms follow. One illustration shows an apparition demanding why William is dressed up like that. William, an eleven-year-old in a respectable family, turns every quiet plan into chaos. Crompton wrote the stories first for adults, then for everyone, and her scruffy hero became a lasting figure of English childhood.
nasa-tm-19690011748-the-use-of-a-ground-:
W. H. Heybey of Marshall Space Flight Center studies crossed-beam wind measurement in this January 1969 memorandum. Experiments were planned at Marshall test sites to measure near-ground winds two ways at once. Tower-mounted anemometers would provide the reference readings. A crossed-beam system combining single-beam and multiple-beam detectors would provide the new measurements.

Heybey studies the beam geometry the system requires. He examines the range of conditions where the geometry physically applies. He then proposes what he considers the best detector arrangement. That arrangement would observe horizontal winds at several heights simultaneously. Better near-ground wind data support launch safety decisions at test sites.
nasa-tm-19700026453-a-method-for-determi:
May T. Meadows of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston wrote this Apollo working paper on September 27, 1963. It gives a method for finding the aerodynamic damping of a rocket's bending modes. The method is applied to the Apollo and Saturn I launch vehicle, whose tall body flexed as it climbed.

Damping tells how quickly air forces calm that bending instead of feeding it. The analysis builds the method step by step, with lift calculations for the bending shapes. Figures show the vehicle, the deflected shapes of its first two bending modes, and the lift each mode's motion creates. Closing charts trace how the damping changes as the rocket passes through rising Mach numbers.
penrod-and-sam:
Booth Tarkington's Penrod and Sam follows Penrod Schofield and Samuel Williams through the game they invented, bonded prisoner. Armed with wooden sabres and imaginary steeds, the boys fence on autumn Saturdays. Whoever is touched becomes a prisoner and must follow his captor's forces until a friend frees him with a sword hilt.

The pursuit sweeps through alleys, stables, yards, and houses at full gallop. Tarkington treats the boys' solemn rules and fierce arguments with perfect seriousness, which is the joke and the charm. The sequel to Penrod is classic American boyhood comedy, exact about how boys actually play.
peter-stuyvesant-the-last-dutch-governor: The sample provided here shows only the analytical contents of John S. C. Abbott's life of Peter Stuyvesant, the chapter summaries, with no narrative text visible. The summaries march from the discovery of America and Hudson's voyage up the river. They pass through the fur trade, forts, and the commencement of colonization, toward the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam and its last governor. Each chapter's events are spelled out in detail, in the manner of Abbott's popular histories for general readers.
podcast-dannyjones-x2z4dXqV9aM:
Mike Hengstebeck returns to Danny Jones for an episode of the KONCRETE Podcast, numbered 63, on the fluid nature of truth, reality, and UFOs. Hengstebeck brings a mind-bending take to the talk. The episode leans more to thought than to case files.

Hengstebeck argues that truth shifts with the mind that holds it, and that UFO lore shows the shift at work. He and Jones roam through tales, doubt, and what counts as real. The talk is loose and deep at once. Listeners who like big questions will find a rich hour. The library holds the episode as an archive record of his stated views.
poetical-works-of-edmund-waller-and-sir-:
Edmund Waller and Sir John Denham share this volume of poetical works, published in 1857 with memoirs and a dissertation by the Reverend George Gilfillan. The life of Waller opens with an essay on why poets' lives are usually dull, and why Waller's was not. He united the supposedly incompatible characters of poet and political plotter, and very nearly reached the gallows as well as Parnassus. Waller was born at Coleshill in March 1605, of an ancient and honorable family.

Waller smoothed English verse with his polished couplets and wrote the age's most quoted panegyrics, while Denham's Cooper's Hill founded the English topographical poem. Both men lived through civil war and trimmed their sails to survive it. Gilfillan pairs them as the twin refiners of the heroic couplet, the craftsmen between Donne's roughness and Pope's perfection, and his notes carry their poems to Victorian readers.
political-thought-in-england-from-locke-:
Harold J. Laski wrote this survey of English political thought from Locke to Bentham for the Home University Library, published in New York and London in 1920. Laski, then a young Harvard historian, opens with a note of debt to Leslie Stephen's history of eighteenth-century thought. A warmer one to his friend Walter Lippmann, with whom he had argued out the book's problems so often that he calls the volume partly a tribute. The task is compression: a century and a half of argument in one small book.

Locke's defense of revolution, the commonwealth men, Hume's skepticism, Burke's reverence, and Bentham's calculus all pass in review, treated as answers to the question of where authority rests. Laski writes with the clarity and quiet radicalism that made him famous. The book remains a model short introduction, brisk, opinionated, and built on the original texts Stephen taught him to dig among.
raspberry-jam:
Raspberry Jam, by Carolyn Wells, is a detective novel in eighteen chapters. The contents name the Emburys and a confession. They name a medium called Marigny. They name Fleming Stone, Wells's gentleman detective, who enters at chapter thirteen. The Great Hanlon of the first chapter is a stage mind-reader about to walk blindfolded through the streets of Newark.

Aunt Abby insists to her niece Eunice that there is something in telepathy. Hanlon, she reads from the paper, will find an article hidden by a man from The Free Press, and the stunt is set for tomorrow. Eunice calls her crazy and doubts that Sanford will take them, but Aunt Abby is determined to go.
scotus-quaestiones-in-metaphysicam:
Scotus's Questions on the Books of the Metaphysics appear here in the 1891 Vives edition of his works. The young Franciscan wrote the questions early in his career, commenting on Aristotle's Metaphysics, the deepest of the ancient texts. Even in this early work, the subtlety that named him the Subtle Doctor is fully present.

The questions ask what being means when said of God and of creatures, and whether one concept can cover both. Scotus answers with his famous claim that being is univocal, said in one sense of all that exists. Oneness, truth, and goodness are sorted with the same care. The Vives printing, a reprint of Wadding's collection, gave the nineteenth century its standard text. Readers meet Scotus the pure thinker here, doing metaphysics as high art.
seventeen-a-tale-of-youth-and-summer-tim:
Booth Tarkington wrote this tale of youth and summer time around the Baxter family, above all William, aged seventeen. Chapter heads trace William's pains: the painful age, sorrows within a boiler, and his father's evening clothes borrowed for love. Little sister Jane watches all with big ears.

Mr. Parcher courts while William suffers the symptoms of first love. Fathers forget, clothes make the man, and time flies in Tarkington's fond satire. The novel catches the agony and vanity of a boy who feels himself a man, set against a family that loves him and laughs at him in equal measure.
some-cities-and-san-francisco-and-resurg:
Hubert Howe Bancroft writes on city rebuilding in Some Cities and San Francisco and Resurgam. Talk of making San Francisco finer had begun before the blow of April 18th, he says. Landscape men had been asked, plans weighed, and first drafts drawn. When fire swept the city that day, the hour to make the needed changes in the rebuilding seemed to have come, and zeal burned warm for a brief time.

Bancroft treats the zeal as a fence held up against fate: let earth shake and fires burn, the city shall rise finer, fairer, and worth more, an imperial city of steel. He then looks back at how great cities grow. Most begin with narrow, bent streets and mean houses, and old towns in Europe and Asia keep the stamp of the castle walls they first rose beneath, as in Edinburgh's old quarter.
tales-of-aztlan-the-romance-of-a-hero-of:
George Hartmann's Tales of Aztlan appears in a revised edition dated 1908. Its subtitle calls it the romance of a hero of the late Spanish-American War. It adds incidents from the life of a western pioneer. Other tales fill out the book. A memorial page states the author's wish: that the volume keep forever fresh the memory of Captain William Owen O'Neill.

A note at the front tells how the final entry, A Maid of Yavapai, is dedicated to Sharlot M. Hall, the famous Arizona settler, and how the author's daughter presented this very copy to her at Prescott, Arizona, in 1942. The contents open with a frail bark tossed on life's tempestuous seas, a perilous journey, and the mystery of a smoking ruin, stalking a warrior and an ambush. Hartmann writes Arizona's pioneer and Rough Rider days as romance.
the-andes-and-the-amazon-or-across-the-c: Title pages alone are present for The Andes and the Amazon, or Across the Continent of South America, by James Orton, professor of natural history at Vassar College in Poughkeepsie, New York. Harper and Brothers of New York printed the book in 1870, with copyright entered the year before. The title promises a new map of equatorial America and many pictures. A front picture is captioned palms on the middle Amazon, and Orton is also named as a corresponding member of the Academy of Natural Sciences at Philadelphia.
the-colonel-s-dream:
Charles W. Chesnutt wrote this novel, published in 1905 by Doubleday of New York and shown here in a Harlem Moon Broadway Books edition. A dedication opens the book, addressed to the great number of people seeking to bring enlightenment to the vexed problems that harass the South. Chesnutt hopes the volume may contribute to that same good end.

He adds a sober reflection on novelty. If nothing new sits between the covers, neither is love new, nor faith, nor hope, nor disappointment, nor sorrow. Life, he argues, is not the less worth living for all that, and no man has truly lived until he has tasted each of them. A list of characters follows, headed by Colonel Henry, though the rest of the list is cut off in what is present.
the-future-of-islam:
Wilfrid Scawen Blunt wrote The Future of Islam as essays first placed in the Fortnightly Review in 1881, printed in book form at London in 1882. Events, he says, forced a quick printing.

Blunt grants the pieces were first sketches for a larger work. Then France seized Tunis, Egypt stirred for reform, and Islam seemed to wake on all sides. He warns that Britain must soon choose in India whether to lead or be led by that wave of faith. The book urges English readers to grasp the forces at work in Muslim lands before they must act in haste.
the-hills-of-hingham: Dallas Lore Sharp wrote The Hills of Hingham. Houghton Mifflin Company published it in Boston and New York. The copyright is dated 1916. The contents list sixteen essays. The titles lean on country life. Examples include The Open Fire and The Ice Crop. Later titles include Seed Catalogues and Spring Ploughing. The list also names The Honey Flow and A Pair of Pigs. The record present here holds front matter only. The essays themselves do not appear.
the-life-of-hon-william-f-cody-known-as-:
William F. Cody told his own life story in an autobiography published in 1879 and dedicated to General Philip H. Sheridan. An introductory note claims the tale reads like romance yet stays truthful. Service under generals Sheridan, Carr, Merritt, and Crook backs that claim, the note argues.

Cody boyhood in troubled Kansas, rides with bull trains, narrow escapes, and pony express work fill the early account. The note insists no brag or humbug mars the man. Readers meet a scout shaped by the plains long before Wild West shows made Buffalo Bill a stage legend.
the-poems-of-henry-kendall-with-biograph: The Poems of Henry Kendall, native-born Australian poet (1841 to 1882), appears with a biographical note by Bertram Stevens. Here only the editorial note and contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. The note explains the edition gathers his three lifetime volumes. It adds pieces from the collected editions of 1886, 1890, and 1903, plus early unreprinted pieces. It also adds poems first printed from his manuscripts in the Mitchell Library. Contents titles include The Muse of Australia, Mountains, Kiama, Song of the Cattle-Hunters, and Bellambi's Maid.
the-rise-of-silas-lapham:
William Dean Howells opens with a newspaper interview. Bartley Hubbard arrives by appointment to see Silas Lapham. The series covers the solid men of Boston. Lapham receives him in a private office. He calls the journalist in through the counting-room door. He does not rise from his desk for the greeting.

Lapham offers a left hand in welcome instead. He rolls his large head toward a vacant chair. He finishes an envelope with a pound of his hairy fist. Then he wheels round in his swivel chair at last. Wealth and bluff manners fill the first scene. Self-making completes the portrait of the paint magnate. Howells builds his study of money and morals here.
the-soul-of-nicholas-snyders-or-the-mise:
Jerome K. Jerome, author of Three Men in a Boat, published this tale with Dodd, Mead and Company in New York in 1909. In Zandam, by the Zuider Zee, the wicked miser Nicholas Snyders lives in the old windmill on the quay. He loves gold only for the power it gives him to tyrannize and oppress.

His whole household is little Christina, an orphan working without wages because Nicholas cleared her dead parents' debts for a few hundred florins. The rich widow Toelast, nearly as miserly as he is, visits and laughs off his proposal that they marry and rule Zandam together. Young sailor Jan Van der Voort, now master of his own ship, is coming to ask for Christina's hand, and Nicholas savours dashing his hopes.
the-sources-and-analogues-of-a-midsummer: Frank Sidgwick compiled this study of Shakespeare's comedy, published in New York by Duffield and Company and in London by Chatto and Windus in 1908. The pages present here give the title page and contents only. An introduction comes first, followed by sections on the main sentimental plot, the grotesque plot, and the fairy plot. Oberon's Vision, illustrative texts, notes, and an index follow, so Sidgwick's argument itself does not appear.
tom-swift-and-his-war-tank-or-doing-his-:
Victor Appleton opens the war tank story with Tom Swift pacing restlessly, then gazing across fields toward factory buildings. Machines there turn out products devised by his father and himself, and a worried look marks the young inventor. Contents promise twenty-five chapters of past memories, indifference, and suspicion.

Neighbours ask whether Tom is a slacker before his tank appears, bridging gaps and entering trenches. Later headings bring a runaway giant, a ruined factory, readiness for France, Tom missing, a prisoner rescued, and camouflage. Readers get a First World War home-front adventure about proving patriotism through invention.
twelve-stories-and-a-dream:
H. G. Wells's Twelve Stories and a Dream leads off with Filmer, a tale of the first flying machine. The contents also promise The Magic Shop, The Valley of Spiders, and The Truth About Pyecraft. A stolen body, a new accelerator, and an inexperienced ghost fill the middle of the list.

Filmer opens by protesting the injustice of fame. Thousands of men built flying piece by piece, yet the popular mind chose one man, who never flew, as discoverer. Poor Filmer, a timid intellectual, pressed the button that changed peace and warfare alike. Wells uses the inventor's smallness against his science's greatness as the story's engine.
yorkshire-ditties-second-series-to-which: John Hartley wrote this second series of Yorkshire ditties, with a dedication to engineer Richard Cherry. A short publisher's preface offers no apology for the volume. Past welcome assured a kind greeting from lovers of the native twang, it says. Pages present here hold that preface and a contents list. Poem titles include Th' Better Part, My Gronfayther's Days, and What It Is to Be Mother. The verses themselves do not appear in these pages.
